lead: Raspberry Pi and Arduino are ready-made boards that hide hardware behind a friendly layer. The Arduino Uno is a microcontroller board: a C++ sketch calls pin and ADC functions that run directly on an ATmega328P. The Raspberry Pi is a single-board computer: a Python program asks a Linux kernel, which runs on a Broadcom SoC, to change a GPIO pin. The choice turns on voltage, analog input, compute and timing. Hobby projects, labs and product prototypes use both.
prereq: You need: Chapters 2.5 and 2.6, and Unit 3 GPIO basics.

blocks.text: A platform is a board plus a software layer that makes pins, timers and buses usable without writing every register. Arduino and Raspberry Pi sit at opposite ends of this idea.

The Arduino Uno carries an ATmega328P: an 8-bit microcontroller (MCU) with 5 V logic, 14 digital pins, 6 analog inputs and a 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC). A C++ sketch calls the Arduino core, and the core writes the MCU registers. The sketch has two functions: setup() runs once, and loop() repeats forever.

The Raspberry Pi is a single-board computer. A Broadcom system on chip (SoC) runs Linux; a 40-pin general-purpose input/output (GPIO) header gives 3.3 V pins but no analog input. A Python or C program in user space asks the kernel to drive a pin. HDMI, USB and network ports make the Pi a small computer, not just a controller.
The figure shows the two stacks. Notice that the 2.5 V sensor reaches only the Arduino ADC path; the Pi needs an external ADC.

sections.h3: Arduino Uno: pins, ADC and timing

blocks.text: The Uno's 14 digital pins are numbered 0 to 13; 6 can produce pulse-width modulation (PWM). The 6 analog inputs are A0 to A5, feeding one 10-bit ADC. The ADC compares the input with a reference, usually 5 V on the Uno. The result is an integer code from 0 to 1023.
The USB bootloader loads the sketch. Then setup() runs once and loop() repeats. The pseudo-code below sets pin 13 as an output, toggles it every 500 ms, reads A0 and prints the code.

blocks.output: Serial monitor at 9600 baud shows one integer per second, between 0 and 1023. A 2.5 V input on A0 with a 5 V reference prints 512.

blocks.text: Timing is more predictable than on Linux because no general-purpose scheduler preempts the loop. Interrupts and library calls still add delay, so the Uno is not a certified hard real-time board.

blocks.where: code is the ADC output (0 to 1023); V<sub>in</sub> is the input voltage in volts; V<sub>ref</sub> is the reference voltage in volts; resolution is the voltage per step in volts.

blocks.text: The divisor 1023 maps the full-scale voltage to the largest code. The divisor 1024 gives the size of one step, or resolution. These two numbers are not interchangeable.

sections.h3: Raspberry Pi: Linux computer with GPIO

blocks.text: The Pi boots Linux from a microSD card. Its GPIO header has 3.3 V logic; a 5 V signal on a pin can damage the SoC. The header has no ADC, so a light sensor or potentiometer needs an external ADC chip, often over I2C or SPI.

A Python program can blink an LED or read a digital sensor. The program does not touch registers; it calls a library, the library calls the kernel, and a driver changes the SoC pin. The same board can show a camera image, log data to a file and send it over Wi-Fi.
Linux is a general-purpose OS. It may pause your program to run another task, so a GPIO pulse can be late by microseconds or more. For a strict deadline, add a small MCU or use a real-time kernel.

Choose the Pi when you need network, storage, camera, display or heavy maths. Choose the Uno when you need 5 V pins, analog input and predictable loop timing at low cost. The Uno is cheaper and draws less power; the Pi costs more and needs a larger supply.

figure.caption: The Arduino path runs a sketch on an ATmega328P and reaches 5 V pins with a 10-bit ADC; the Pi path runs Python on Linux over a Broadcom SoC and reaches 3.3 V GPIO with no ADC. The 2.5 V sensor connects only to the Arduino ADC.

spec.title: Two platform stacks
spec.aria: Two software stacks run an Arduino sketch on an ATmega328P and a Python program on Linux over a Broadcom SoC, and a 2.5 V sensor reaches only the Arduino ADC.

examples.question: An Arduino Uno uses its 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference. A sensor outputs 2.5 V. Find the ADC code and the resolution in mV. Use code = round(V<sub>in</sub> × 1023 ÷ V<sub>ref</sub>).
steps: List values: V<sub>in</sub> = 2.5 V, V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V, bits = 10, so full-scale code = 2<sup>10</sup> - 1 = 1023.
Round to the nearest integer code: 512.
examples.answer: The ADC code is 512 and the resolution is 4.8828125 mV (about 4.88 mV).
examples.check:
Vref = 5.0
Vin = 2.5
code_float = Vin * 1023 / Vref
code = round(code_float)
resolution_mV = Vref / 1024 * 1000
print(code_float)
print(code)
print(resolution_mV)

traps: Raspberry Pi GPIO is 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant; a 5 V sensor signal can damage the SoC.
The Raspberry Pi has no built-in ADC; an analog sensor needs an external ADC chip.
Linux makes the Pi a general-purpose computer, not a hard real-time controller; GPIO pulses can jitter.
For a 10-bit ADC, the largest code is 1023, but resolution uses 1024 steps; do not write 5 V ÷ 1023 for resolution.
The Arduino Uno has an 8-bit MCU with small RAM and flash; heavy maths, camera work or networking usually needs a Pi or a host PC.

quiz.q: Which microcontroller is on the Arduino Uno, and what is its logic voltage?
Why does the Raspberry Pi need an external ADC for a potentiometer?
quiz.a: The Pi GPIO header has digital pins only; it has no built-in ADC. The potentiometer gives an analog voltage, so an external ADC converts it to a digital value.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC on an Arduino Uno has V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V. A sensor gives 1.25 V. Find the code using round(V<sub>in</sub> × 1023 ÷ V<sub>ref</sub>).
Why is a Python GPIO pulse on a Raspberry Pi less predictable than an Arduino loop pulse?
quiz.a: Linux schedules many processes and may preempt the Python program; the Arduino loop runs on bare metal with no general-purpose OS scheduler. Both can be interrupted, but the Pi has more jitter.

quiz.q: State the Raspberry Pi GPIO logic voltage and the number of analog inputs on the Pi header.
What is the difference between setup() and loop() in an Arduino sketch?
quiz.a: setup() runs once after reset and sets pins and ports; loop() runs repeatedly after setup().

quiz.q: A project must stream camera images over Wi-Fi and also produce a precise 10 µs trigger pulse every 1 ms. Which platform or combination do you choose, and why?
quiz.a: Use a Raspberry Pi for the camera and Wi-Fi, plus a small MCU such as an Arduino for the 10 µs pulse. Linux alone gives poor microsecond timing; the MCU gives a predictable loop or timer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses Arduino-style boards for quick control prototypes and Pi-class boards for gateways, vision and dashboards. Many products use a Pi as a Linux host plus a small MCU for deterministic I/O. Search for Raspberry Pi GPIO 3.3 V, Arduino ADC resolution, and real-time Linux PREEMPT_RT.
